---
title: "Sigma-algebras"
---

Suppose that our pronoun model can measure whether a form is plural. The same model must also be able to measure whether the form is not plural, since the second event is the complement of the first. A collection of measurable events must therefore have a particular structure.

This requirement motivates a [**sigma-algebra**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_%28Siegrist%29/01%3A_Foundations/1.11%3A_Measurable_Spaces), also called an event space. A sigma-algebra is the collection of events to which a probability model can assign probabilities. We write this collection as $\mathcal{F}$.

To see why the collection needs structure, use the four outcome sample space

$$
\Omega_4
=\{\textit{he},\textit{him},\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

Let $P$ be the plural event:

$$
P=\{\textit{they},\textit{them}\}.
$$

Its complement is

$$
P^c=\{\textit{he},\textit{him}\}.
$$

If plural number is the only distinction that the model measures, one possible sigma-algebra is

$$
\mathcal{F}_P
=\{\varnothing,P,P^c,\Omega_4\}.
$$

This collection lets us ask whether a pronoun is plural or singular. It does not let us ask whether the pronoun is accusative, because the accusative event is not in $\mathcal{F}_P$.

## Closure requirements

A sigma-algebra must remain coherent when we negate or combine measurable questions. It satisfies three requirements.

1. The complete sample space $\Omega$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.
2. If $B$ belongs to $\mathcal{F}$, then its complement $B^c$ also belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.
3. If $B_1,B_2,\ldots$ belong to $\mathcal{F}$, then their union $\bigcup_i B_i$ also belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.

The first requirement makes the certain event measurable. The second makes the complement of every measurable event measurable. The third makes any countable union of measurable events measurable.

These requirements also supply events that were not listed directly. Since $\Omega\in\mathcal{F}$, closure under complements gives

$$
\Omega^c=\varnothing\in\mathcal{F}.
$$

Intersections follow from complements and unions. De Morgan's law gives

$$
B\cap C=(B^c\cup C^c)^c.
$$

Thus a sigma-algebra that is closed under complements and countable unions is also closed under intersections.

## A collection that is not a sigma-algebra

Consider the proposed collection

$$
\mathcal{G}=\{\Omega_4,P\}.
$$

The three requirements provide a direct test.

1. It contains $\Omega_4$, so it passes the first requirement.
2. It contains $P$ but not $P^c$, so it fails the second requirement.
3. It also lacks $\varnothing$, which must appear as $\Omega_4^c$.

Adding $P^c$ and $\varnothing$ repairs these failures and produces $\mathcal{F}_P$.

We can encode the four events in base R. The code does not establish the general mathematical definition, but it lets us inspect this finite case.

```{r}
#| eval: false
omega <- c("he", "him", "they", "them")
plural <- c("they", "them")
singular <- setdiff(omega, plural)

event_space <- list(
  impossible = character(0),
  plural = plural,
  singular = singular,
  certain = omega
)

event_space
```

The list omits the singleton event $\{\textit{them}\}$. This set is a subset of $\Omega_4$, but it is not an event in $\mathcal{F}_P$. The model therefore represents *them* as an outcome without assigning a probability to the event that isolates it.

## Sample spaces and event spaces

The sample space and sigma-algebra answer different representation questions.

1. $\Omega$ states which individual outcomes exist in the model.
2. $\mathcal{F}$ states which groupings of those outcomes can receive probabilities.

For a small finite sample space, we will often use the power set $2^\Omega$, the collection containing every subset of $\Omega$. In that case, every possible grouping of the represented outcomes is measurable. The smaller sigma-algebra $\mathcal{F}_P$ shows that this choice is not automatic.

## Nonmeasurable scientific questions

A scientific question may require an event that is not measurable under the declared sigma-algebra. This occurs when the analysis asks for the probability of a set that does not belong to $\mathcal{F}$.

In the example above, an analysis might report a probability for accusative case even though the model measures only number. No numerical estimate can repair this problem, because the accusative set has not been included among the events to which the model assigns probabilities.

For the finite examples in this course, taking $\mathcal{F}=2^\Omega$ will usually close the gap. We still write $\mathcal{F}$ separately because the distinction becomes important when the outcome space is not finite.

## Check your understanding

1. Start with $\{\Omega_4,P\}$. Which two events must be added to obtain $\mathcal{F}_P$?
2. Is $\{\varnothing,\Omega_4\}$ a sigma-algebra? Check all three requirements.
3. Why does $\{\textit{them}\}\subseteq\Omega_4$ not guarantee that $\{\textit{them}\}\in\mathcal{F}_P$?
4. Use De Morgan's law to explain why closure under complements and unions gives closure under intersections.

We have constructed one sigma-algebra by inspection. The [next page](generating-event-spaces.qmd) gives a systematic procedure for constructing the smallest sigma-algebra that contains a specified set of linguistic distinctions.
